lines: \paragraph{Reasoning depth.} An ablation comparing chain-of-thought reasoning against direct-answer generation on 6 task types ($n{=}120$ episodes per condition, 6 tasks $\times$ 20 episodes per task) found no significant difference (Mann--Whitney $p > 0.26$, $|d| \leq 0.31$) and near-identical death rates (41.8\% vs.\ 42.5\%); reasoning depth does not meaningfully alter internal-mode outcomes.

+Given per-task death risk knowledge, we test whether a simple threshold routing strategy can outperform always-deterministic. For each threshold $t \in [0, 1]$, we route to internal if the per-task internal death rate $\leq t$, otherwise to deterministic, and sweep all thresholds to find the optimal.
+Strategy & Mean Score & Death Rate & $\Delta$ vs Det \\

+\caption{Death-risk threshold routing analysis on 245 episodes. The optimal threshold routes only \texttt{find-non-living-thing} (the sole zero-death task) to internal, with all other tasks routed to deterministic. Bootstrap 95\% CI for the difference: $[-8.87, +5.92]$.}

+Even with perfect per-task death risk knowledge, threshold routing cannot outperform always-deterministic. The sole zero-death task achieves higher scores under deterministic (+28.5) than internal (+18.9), leaving no room for a beneficial mixed strategy.

lines: The $r = 0.97$ correlation is specific to catastrophic death ($P{=}100$); defining failure as any non-positive score yields $r = -0.13$ ($p = 0.70$). As shown in \S\ref{sec:death-decomp}, this correlation follows algebraically from death dominance when $P$ is constant; larger models with lower death rates would reduce DAF. This prediction assumes models above a minimum capability threshold; preliminary evidence (Qwen2.5-0.5B, $N{=}15$) suggests very weak models may exhibit low death rates not from avoidance ability but from inability to reach dangerous states.

-Death avoidance dominance (78.9\% of non-tie labels, DAF $= 90.4\%$ at $P{=}100$) reframes modality routing as a \emph{safety} problem, closer to a conservative default policy than to cost-quality optimization~\citep{garcia2015comprehensive, cogrouter-2026}. The underlying failure mechanism is state hallucination: the internal strategy predicts that an action succeeded when the environment state did not change, leading to cascading errors that trigger death. The deterministic strategy eliminates these compounding observation errors, while action-selection errors (16.3\% deterministic death rate) remain comparatively rare. The 86:9 label imbalance explains why always-deterministic is a strong baseline; 4B parameters for $+9$\,pp router improvement is consistent with the analytical framework being more efficient.

The deterministic strategy eliminates these compounding observation errors, while action-selection errors (16.3\% deterministic death rate) remain comparatively rare. The 86:9 label imbalance explains why always-deterministic is a strong baseline; 4B parameters for $+9$\,pp router improvement is consistent with the analytical framework being more efficient. This dominance is so thorough that even an oracle routing strategy with perfect per-task death risk knowledge cannot outperform always-deterministic (Appendix~\ref{sec:threshold-routing}, Table~\ref{tab:threshold-routing}).

The framework applies most directly to environments with sparse terminal rewards and catastrophic failure modes. Environments with graded failure costs would yield intermediate DAF values; stronger backbones with lower hallucination rates would reduce death-rate differentials and consequently lower DAF.
